Thursday, October 15, 2026 Daily Digest

86% of B2B Buyers Purchased AI Agent Software, Stagwell and ServiceNow Launch AI Marketing Partnership, Agent Governance Market Emerges

Today's top stories in AI + enterprise tech

1

G2 Research: 86% of B2B Software Buyers Purchased AI Agent Software in Past Year, Up 25%

New research from G2 reveals that AI agents have moved decisively from pilot to production, with 86% of B2B software buyers reporting they purchased AI agent software or services in the past year — a 25% increase from the prior period. The research also highlights a growing tension: while AI agents are increasingly embedded in production environments, effective oversight comes at a significant cost. Organizations are discovering that the agent deployment question isn't just "can we?" but "how do we govern it?" The findings track with Gartner's projection that 40% of enterprise applications will integrate with task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from less than 5% in 2025. What's notable is the speed: in less than 18 months, AI agents have gone from a capability that required explanation to a line item on most enterprise software budgets. The "oversight cost" the research identifies — staff, tools, and process changes needed to manage autonomous systems — is the next budget line that procurement teams are learning to estimate.

2

Stagwell and ServiceNow Announce 3-Year AI Marketing Partnership to Close the "Execution Gap"

Stagwell, the challenger agency network, and ServiceNow announced a three-year collaboration to "modernize how enterprises build, activate, and measure marketing campaigns." The partnership positions ServiceNow as what the companies call "the Super Intelligence Control Tower for business reinvention" — a framing that signals how enterprise workflow platforms are repositioning as the orchestration layer for AI-driven marketing. The announcement addresses what both companies describe as the AI-marketing execution gap: the distance between the AI capabilities marketers have access to and their ability to actually deploy those capabilities at scale within enterprise governance constraints. ServiceNow brings workflow automation, approval routing, and audit capabilities; Stagwell brings creative and media execution. Together, they're betting that enterprise marketing's next phase isn't about more AI tools but about connecting AI tools to the approval chains, brand governance, and measurement infrastructure that large organizations require. For CMOs watching the partnership unfold, the question is whether this becomes a reference architecture for AI-enabled marketing operations or another case study that applies only to organizations with ServiceNow already in their stack.

3

SpringBrand Ships AI Agent Builder: GTM Teams Build Agents by Describing Tasks in Plain English

SpringBrand launched an AI agent builder that lets marketing, sales, and support teams create agents by describing the task rather than drawing a workflow graph. The platform offers access to more than 10,000 APIs and plugins through a single account, with ready-to-use workflows for over 500 go-to-market scenarios covering SEO automation, competitor analysis, content creation, meeting prep, lead qualification, and CRM work. The launch reflects a broader market shift: as agents become mainstream (per G2's 86% figure), demand has shifted from "build agents for developers" to "build agents for marketers." SpringBrand's architecture — describe the task, let the agent find the right plugins, approve before execution — is designed for users who know the work but don't want to learn n8n or Zapier node structures. The company cited Gartner's forecast that 40% of enterprise applications will integrate task-specific AI agents by year-end. What SpringBrand is betting on is that the integration work — connecting agents to data sources and execution endpoints — can be abstracted into a "describe and run" interface rather than a visual workflow builder. Whether that abstraction holds up for enterprise use cases with complex approval chains remains to be tested.

4

Harbor Raises $10M to Manage AI Agent Risk as Governance Layer Emerges

Harbor emerged from stealth with $10 million in funding to focus specifically on mitigating the risks associated with deploying AI agents. The San Francisco-based company represents a new category forming around AI agent governance — distinct from model security, prompt injection protection, or data loss prevention. The thesis: as agents proliferate and gain autonomous capabilities, organizations need dedicated infrastructure to answer questions like "what can this agent access?" and "what did it do, and why?" Harbor joins Opsin, which launched its Guardian Agent Platform this week to discover and govern AI agents across enterprises, mapping data connections, assessing risks, and enforcing policies. The pattern emerging is familiar from earlier technology waves: first capability, then adoption, then governance. Enterprise security and compliance teams are now asking for the tools to audit agent actions, control credential surfaces, and enforce policies on what agents can do — questions that existing security tooling wasn't designed to answer. The $10M raise is modest by AI startup standards, but the category Harbor is entering addresses a pain point that intensifies with every agent deployment.

5

Bloomberg Opens ASKB Agentic AI to All 375,000 Terminal Users

Bloomberg told WSJ CIO Journal it is extending its ASKB conversational AI system from a beta subset to all 375,000 Terminal users, and will allow subscribers to integrate their own documents and data alongside Bloomberg's financial content. Each ASKB response includes citations to underlying BQL formulas or source documents — a design choice Bloomberg says keeps the tool usable in regulated capital-markets workflows where audit trails matter. ASKB uses an orchestrated multi-agent architecture rather than a single large model, with different agents handling different aspects of queries. The move represents Bloomberg's bet that financial professionals want AI integrated into their existing workflows rather than as a separate interface. For regulated industries more broadly, the citation and audit trail design offers a template: AI that can answer questions and take actions, but with the provenance and traceability that compliance requires. The expansion also signals confidence that ASKB has cleared whatever internal quality bar Bloomberg set during beta — a meaningful datapoint given the reputational stakes Bloomberg faces if financial professionals act on incorrect AI-generated information.

💡 My Take

The agent market just grew up. When 86% of B2B software buyers report purchasing AI agent software — up 25% in a single year — you're no longer tracking an emerging trend. You're watching a market become infrastructure. But today's news also shows what maturity actually looks like. Harbor's $10M raise and Opsin's Guardian platform aren't about agent capabilities; they're about agent accountability. Stagwell and ServiceNow's partnership isn't about creativity; it's about connecting AI to approval chains and audit trails. Bloomberg's ASKB expansion isn't about chat; it's about citations and provenance. The pattern across all five stories is the same: capability is now assumed, so the competitive surface has shifted to governance, integration, and trust. SpringBrand's bet — that marketers can build agents by describing tasks — works only if the governance layer is also invisible or at least manageable. The question enterprise leaders should be asking isn't "should we deploy agents?" (the G2 data says most already have), but "do we have the oversight infrastructure to know what those agents are doing?" Harbor, Opsin, and Bloomberg's citation system are early answers. More will follow. The agent market has graduated from "can it work?" to "can we control it?" That's usually when the enterprise budgets start flowing in earnest.
